goal: Reduce full graph encoder inference latency for the standard workload, preserving the full output checks.
completion: One measured invocation is exactly one complete graph encoder forward: infer(model, inputs) (infer.py:28-30), i.e. model(features, sources, destinations, degree) under @torch.inference_mode(). The framework's completion boundary is CUDA synchronization on both sides of run(state) with wall-clock timing (mirroring infer.py:53-58); run() returns the full FP32 output tensor of shape [nodes, output_features] = [4096, 64]. Model/fixture construction, warmup, quality checking and statistics queries are outside the timed boundary.
state_protocol: prepare(context, request) reproduces infer.py:12-25 outside timing: torch.set_num_threads(4), torch.manual_seed(20261021), TF32 disabled (cuda.matmul and cudnn), torch.set_float32_matmul_precision('highest'), GraphEncoder(128, 256, 64) built on CPU then moved to context['device'] and set to eval(); the input fixture is built with a CPU generator seeded seed+1 (features randn, sources/destinations randint over nodes, degree = bincount(destinations, minlength=nodes).float()), then moved to the device; nodes and edges are read from request['workload']. Model and inputs are kept in the returned state dict. Inference has no cross-invocation state (README.md:17-18), so reset(state) is a no-op: run() creates its own request-local state via the inference_mode context and mutates nothing. run(state) executes the single forward and returns its output tensor. observe(state, result) returns the complete detached output tensor on CPU. metrics(state, result, elapsed_ms) returns latency_ms = elapsed_ms, graphs_per_second = 1000/elapsed_ms and (mirroring the source sample fields) peak_allocated_bytes from torch.cuda.max_memory_allocated() queried outside the timer after the framework's post-run synchronization. models(state) exposes the loaded GraphEncoder root module for discovery/replacement. set_mode records the mode; execution is identical in quality/measure/profile because the full output is always produced.
invariants: FP32 weights and features (workloads.json dtype float32); TF32 disabled via torch.backends.cuda.matmul.allow_tf32 = False and torch.backends.cudnn.allow_tf32 = False, and torch.set_float32_matmul_precision('highest') (infer.py:13-18).

Model architecture is fixed: two-layer mean GraphSAGE GraphEncoder with input_features=128, hidden_features=256, output_features=64, ReLU between layers, each layer projecting concat(self features, mean neighbor features) with nn.Linear (model.py).
model.eval() plus forward under @torch.inference_mode(); no cross-invocation state (infer.py:18,28-30).

Seeded fixtures reproduced exactly: torch.manual_seed(20261021) before model construction; a CPU torch.Generator seeded 20271021 (seed+1) produces features = randn(nodes, 128), sources = randint(nodes, (edges,)), destinations = randint(nodes, (edges,)); degree = torch.bincount(destinations, minlength=nodes).float() (infer.py:14-25, workloads.json seed).

Graph semantics: duplicate directed edges contribute individually via index_add_ on a zeros_like base; nodes without incoming edges keep zero neighbor features; neighbor mean divides by degree.clamp_min(1).unsqueeze(1) (model.py:11-15, README.md:17-19).

Quality check: the complete FP32 output tensor (shape [4096, 64] for the standard workload) compared with torch.testing.assert_close(atol=1e-5, rtol=1e-4); output is continuous floating point with no discrete outputs (infer.py:44-45, workloads.json quality).
One run() equals exactly one infer(model, inputs) forward on GPU-resident tensors; the full workload must be executed even though the objective is a single latency number.

Workload dimensions (nodes=4096, edges=65536) are read from request['workload'] in prepare(), not embedded as constants; the held-out unseen_graph workload (7168 nodes, 143360 edges) is not part of this request.
Single-process, single-device workload: model and inputs live on context['device']; no distributed backend and no communication (request devices/communication).
assumptions: The adapter reads model dimensions and the seed from the source workloads.json when it can be located (request source_root, inputs/source, or the adapter directory); otherwise it falls back to constants identical to the source values (input_features=128, hidden_features=256, output_features=64, seed=20261021), which are fixed architecture/policy constants rather than workload-dependent values.

latency_ms is wall-clock time around one forward with CUDA synchronization at both boundaries; the framework timer supplies this, so run() performs no internal synchronization, matching the source where sync and perf_counter_ns live in the harness loop (infer.py:53-58).

The framework resets CUDA peak memory stats immediately before its timer, so metrics() queries torch.cuda.max_memory_allocated() after run to mirror the source's per-sample peak_allocated_bytes field (infer.py:60).
graphs_per_second = 1000/latency_ms is derived in metrics() from the unchanged work amount (one full forward) and elapsed_ms, matching infer.py:59.

observe() returns the full output tensor (the source's only correctness artifact, torch.save of the complete tensor at infer.py:47); required_observations is empty and no communication collectors apply.
The peak_allocated_bytes goal declared in workloads.json is not part of this request; the user goal selects latency_ms only (request notes).
